content: Neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE) is a passively transferred autoimmune condition that occurs in approximately 1-2% of infants born to mothers with autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or Sjögren’s syndrome. This condition is associated with maternal autoantibodies, particularly anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. The most severe complication of neonatal lupus is congenital complete heart block. The first documented case of neonatal lupus was reported in 1928 by Aylward, who described two siblings with congenital heart block born to a mother with Sjögren’s syndrome. In 1945, Plant and Stevens identified congenital heart block as a manifestation of neonatal lupus. McCuistion and Schoch, in 1954, were the first to link maternal autoimmune disease with cutaneous lupus in the infant. By 1957, Hogg suggested a connection between maternal autoimmune disease and congenital heart block in offspring. Finally, in 1980, Weston established the association between neonatal lupus and maternal anti-Ro autoantibodies. The pathophysiology of neonatal lupus is believed to involve the transplacental transfer of maternal anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. These antibodies target Ro and La molecules, which are components of a single particle present in all cells. Recent research has explored the role of microchimerism, a phenomenon where fetal cells persist in the mother (fetal microchimerism) and maternal cells persist in the offspring (maternal microchimerism). This cell transfer during pregnancy may contribute to autoimmune diseases, including neonatal lupus. Notably, maternal microchimerism has been identified in the hearts of male infants with neonatal lupus who succumbed to congenital heart block. Genetic predisposition also plays a role in neonatal lupus. Specific HLA alleles, such as DQB102 and DRB103, and a polymorphism in the promoter region of the tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) gene (-308A, associated with increased TNF-α production), have been implicated in the development of skin manifestations. The primary cause of neonatal lupus is the presence of maternal autoantibodies, particularly anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies, which cross the placenta. These antibodies are responsible for 60-90% of cases of congenital complete heart block. In rare cases, maternal antibodies to other antigens, such as anti-U1 RNP antibodies, have been implicated in the absence of anti-SSA/Ro or anti-SSB/La antibodies. Microchimerism, as mentioned earlier, may also contribute to the pathogenesis. Neonatal lupus must be differentiated from other conditions that cause atrioventricular (AV) block, such as familial conduction disorders or congenital structural heart disease. In cases without neonatal lupus, familial inheritance of conduction disease is often the underlying cause of AV block. The prevalence of anti-SSA antibodies in women is approximately 1 in 200, but the incidence of neonatal lupus is much lower, at about 1 in 20,000 live births. Only 1-2% of infants born to mothers with anti-SSA/Ro antibodies, with or without anti-SSB/La antibodies, develop neonatal lupus. However, the risk increases to 3% if the mother has both anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La antibodies. If the mother has SLE in addition to anti-SSA antibodies, the incidence of neonatal lupus rises to 6-13%. The risk is even higher, up to 25%, if the mother has previously given birth to a child with neonatal lupus. Among affected infants, 15-20% present with complete heart block, while 6% present with cutaneous lupus. Congenital heart block occurs in 50-60% of cases, cutaneous lupus in 25-30%, and a combination of cardiac and cutaneous manifestations in 4-10%. The most significant risk factor for congenital heart block is the presence of maternal anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. Other risk factors include maternal anti-U1 RNP antibodies and fetal genetic factors. Prenatal screening for anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La antibodies is recommended for women at risk, such as those with lupus, Sjögren’s syndrome, undifferentiated autoimmune diseases, or a history of giving birth to a child with neonatal lupus. The natural history of neonatal lupus varies. The characteristic rash typically resolves without scarring within six to eight months. The appearance of skin lesions is unrelated to breastfeeding, and breastfeeding is not contraindicated in mothers with anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. Infants with asymptomatic complete heart block often remain stable until later childhood, adolescence, or adulthood. However, without pacing, exercise limitations and even death may occur. The prognosis for children who receive pacemaker implantation is generally excellent, although heart failure may develop in some cases. Diagnosis of neonatal lupus involves identifying maternal anti-SSA/Ro and SSB/La autoantibodies. Pregnant women who test positive for these antibodies may benefit from frequent fetal echocardiographic monitoring to assess for fetal heart block. Fetal bradycardia, indicative of complete or second-degree AV block, can be detected through routine fetal auscultation, ultrasonography, or echocardiography. Medical management of neonatal lupus includes prenatal treatment with fluorinated glucocorticoids for mothers of fetuses with second-degree heart block, continuing through pregnancy based on the response. Prophylactic treatment with hydroxychloroquine (400 mg orally once daily) is recommended for pregnant women with anti-SSA/Ro antibodies who have previously given birth to a child with cardiac manifestations of neonatal lupus, regardless of the mother’s health status. Surgical intervention, specifically pacemaker placement, is the primary therapeutic decision after the perinatal period for infants with complete heart block.
